Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 97, verse 1:

﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree.﴾

This verse contains a great honouring of the Qur'an. It opens with the particle (inna) and with a predication expressed by a verbal sentence; both are among the means of emphasis and reinforcement.

This fronting (al-taqdim) yields restriction (qasr), specifically qasr qalb (restriction by reversal), in response to the polytheists who denied that the Qur'an was sent down from God, Exalted is He.

In the pronoun of majesty (damir al-'azama) and in attributing the sending down to Him there is a great honouring of the Qur'an.

In the use of the pronoun for the Qur'an rather than the explicit noun there is an indication that it is present in the minds of the Muslims because of their intense devotion to it. The pronoun, without a preceding referent, is thus an indication of its fame among them. It is therefore permissible that by it is meant the whole Qur'an, and the verb (anzalna) is then used for the beginning of the sending down, because what was sent down on that night was the first five verses of Surat al-'Alaq. Then revelation paused, then its sending down resumed in stages (munajjaman), and the sending down of the Qur'an was not completed until after more than twenty years. However, since the whole Qur'an, its measure and the fact that it would be sent down upon the Prophet ﷺ in stages until it was complete, was determined in the knowledge of God, Exalted is He, its sending down is regarded as having occurred with the sending down of its first verses; for what is attached to a thing is considered as being in the position of its beginning. The Prophet ﷺ said: "A prayer in this mosque of mine is better than a thousand prayers in any other," and the hadith continues. The scholars agreed that the reward (al-surra) for what has been added to the Prophetic Mosque has that same merit, and that circumambulation (al-tawaf) in the additions to the Sacred Mosque is valid whenever the mosque is expanded.

Among the precision of the arrangement of the Mushaf is that Surat al-Qadr was placed right after Surat al-'Alaq, even though it has fewer verses than Surat al-Bayyina and the surahs after it. It is as if this were an indication that the pronoun in (anzalnahu) refers to the Qur'an whose revelation began with Surat al-'Alaq.

It is also permissible that the pronoun refers to the measure that was sent down on that night, which is the five verses of Surat al-'Alaq; for every part of the Qur'an is called Qur'an. On both interpretations, the use of the past tense in the verb (anzalnahu) is not metaphorical. It has been said that the pronoun of the Qur'an was applied to a part of it metaphorically, by the relation of partness.

The verse clearly states that the first verses of the Qur'an were sent down at night, which is what the hadith of the beginning of revelation in the Two Sahihs requires, in 'A'isha's words in it: "He would seclude himself (yatahannath) in the Cave of Hira' for many nights," so his worship was at night. It seems that the angel descended upon him immediately after he finished his worship. As for 'A'isha's words, "The Messenger of God returned with it, his heart trembling," their meaning is that he came out of the Cave of Hira' at dawn after the end of his instruction in the five verses, since their descent upon him would then be at the end of that night, and that is the best time of the night, as God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿and those who seek forgiveness at dawn﴾ [Al 'Imran: 17].

Laylat al-Qadr (the Night of Decree): a name that God gave to the night in which the sending down of the Qur'an began. It seems that the first time it was called by this name was in this verse, and it was not known among the Muslims; and by this, its mention with this name is a way of arousing curiosity about knowing it. Therefore he followed it with: ﴿And what will make you know what the Night of Decree is?﴾ [al-Qadr: 2].

Al-qadr: the word by which the night is defined through the idafa (annexation) is in the sense of nobility and excellence, as God, Exalted is He, said in Surat al-Dukhan: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down in a blessed night﴾ [al-Dukhan: 3], that is, the Night of Decree and of nobility with God, Exalted is He, because of the blessing He bestowed upon it. That is a night which God gave honour, and made it a manifestation of what His knowledge had preceded, so He made it the beginning of revelation to the Prophet ﷺ.

The definiteness of al-qadr is the definiteness of the genus (ta'rif al-jins). He did not say "in a night of qadr" with indefiniteness, because he intended to make this compound stand in the position of a proper name for that night, like a proper name by dominance (al-'alam bi-l-ghalaba); for the definiteness of the annexed noun by the article together with the definiteness of the annexing noun by the annexation is more emphatic in making that compound a title (laqab), since two definitions are combined in it.

It is established that the beginning of the sending down of the Qur'an was in the month of Ramadan, as God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was sent down, a guidance for mankind and clear proofs of guidance and criterion﴾ [al-Baqara: 185]. There is no doubt that the Muslims knew this, since the revelation of this surah was years before the revelation of Surat al-Baqara if the surah is Meccan, or by a shorter period if the surah is Medinan. So the Night of Decree intended here was in Ramadan, and this is confirmed by the authentic reports that it falls among the nights of Ramadan every year.

Most of the narrations say that the night in which the Qur'an was sent down upon the Prophet ﷺ was the night of the seventeenth of Ramadan. What comes later in the interpretation of the verses, after these words, concerns whether the night has a fixed number that is the same in all years or varies across the years; whether it falls on any of the nights of Ramadan or does not go beyond the last ten of it; and whether it is specific to an odd night, as it was the first time, or is not specific to that. The purpose of honouring the night in which the beginning of the sending down of the Qur'an occurred is another honouring of the Qur'an, by honouring the time of its appearance, drawing attention to the fact that God, Exalted is He, chose for the beginning of its sending down a noble and blessed time; for the greatness of the act requires that for its occurrence one choose the excellent times and places. So the choice of excellent times for the beginning of its sending down indicates the elevation of its rank with God, Exalted is He, like His saying: ﴿None touches it except the purified﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 79], according to both interpretations of the meaning of "the purified."

A cautionary indication in the form of ambiguity, meaning that grasping its reality is not easy, because of the many virtues it contains.

The expression "*ma adraka ma kadha*" (what will make you know what such-and-such is) is used to magnify and exalt a thing. The meaning is: what informs you of what the Night of Decree is? That is, it is difficult for anything to inform you of its extent. This has been mentioned more than once before, such as His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what the Day of Judgment is?﴾ [Al-Infitar: 17], in Surat al-Infitar, shortly before. The *waw* is the *waw* of the circumstantial clause (*waw al-hal*).

The name "﴿the Night of Decree﴾ [Al-Qadr: 3]" is repeated, having been mentioned shortly before in His saying: ﴿in the Night of Decree﴾ [Al-Qadr: 1], contrary to what the apparent structure would require, since the apparent structure would call for a pronoun. He intended to give it emphasis by specifying it. Thus the exaltation of the Night of Decree is stated explicitly, and there is an indirect expression of the exaltation of what was revealed in it, and that God chose its revelation to occur in it, so that the two nobilities correspond.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 97, verse 3:

Page 459
﴿The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months.﴾
This is a first clarification of some of the vagueness in His words: ﴿And what will make you know what the Night of Decree is?﴾ [al-Qadr: 2], similar to the clarification in His words: ﴿And what will make you know what the steep path is? [It is] freeing a slave﴾ [al-Balad: 12-13], or feeding, and the verse continues. Therefore the sentence is detached (fasl), because it is a clarifying resumption (istinaf bayani), or because it functions like an appositive (atf al-bayan).

Its being preferred as "better than a thousand months" is only by multiplying the reward of the righteous deeds performed in it, the answering of supplication, the abundance of the reward of charities, and the blessing it brings to the Ummah. This is because the superiority of days does not depend on the measure of their durations, nor on what occurs in them of heat, cold, or rain, nor on their being long or short; for those conditions are not regarded by Allah the Exalted. Rather, Allah regards the good that results for people, individually and collectively, and what aids the truth, goodness, and the spread of the religion. He has said regarding the superiority of people: ﴿Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you﴾. Likewise, the superiority of times is measured only by what occurs in them, because they are containers for deeds and do not possess intrinsic qualities by which they could be superior to one another as people are. So their excellence lies in what Allah has designated for them of preference, like the preference of the last third of the night for acts of devotion. The number "thousand" appears to be used to denote abundance of multiplication, as in his saying: "one who is equal to a thousand" (wahid ka-alf), and upon this came His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Each one of them wishes he could be granted a life of a thousand years﴾ [al-Baqarah: 96]. The number of abundance is specified here with "months" for the sake of rhyme with the final letter, the ra'.

In the Muwatta: "Malik said: he heard from one he trusts among the people of knowledge who said: 'The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was shown the lifespans of the people before him, or what Allah willed of that, and it seemed that the lifespans of his Ummah were too short for them to reach the same amount of deeds as others reached in long life, so Allah gave him the Night of Decree, which is better than a thousand months.'" End quote.

The expression of the phrase (﴿Laylat al-Qadr﴾) in a place where a pronoun would be expected is for emphasis, and this phrase is repeated three times; the three repetitions are generally where repetition ends, as in His saying, exalted is He: "And indeed, among them is a party who distort their tongues with the Book, that you may think it is from the Book, but it is not from the Book."

And the saying of 'Adi:

"I do not see death overtaking death; something has made death bitter for the rich and the poor."

It is worth drawing attention to what occurred in the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi with its chain to al-Qasim ibn al-Fadl
Page 460
al-Huddani, from Yusuf ibn Sa'd, who said: "A man stood before al-Hasan ibn 'Ali after he had pledged allegiance to Mu'awiyah and said: 'You have blackened the faces of the believers,' or 'O blackener of the faces of the believers!' He said: 'Do not reproach me, may Allah have mercy on you; the Prophet ﷺ was shown the Banu Umayyah on his pulpit, and that grieved him, so there was revealed: ﴿Indeed, We have granted you al-Kawthar﴾ [al-Kawthar: 1], meaning a river in Paradise, and there was revealed: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾ [al-Qadr: 1], ﴿And what will make you know what the Night of Decree is?﴾ [al-Qadr: 2], ﴿The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months﴾, which the Banu Umayyah will rule, O Muhammad.'" Al-Qasim said: "We counted it, and it came to exactly a thousand months, not gaining a day or losing a day." Abu 'Isa al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a gharib hadith; we do not know it except through this route. It has been related from al-Qasim ibn al-Fadl from Yusuf ibn Mazin, and al-Qasim ibn al-Fadl is trustworthy, while Yusuf ibn Sa'd is an unknown man." End quote.

Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir: Ibn Jarir narrated it through the route of al-Qasim ibn al-Fadl from 'Isa ibn Mazin, so he said, and 'Isa ibn Mazin is not known, and this implies disturbance (idtirab) in this hadith, that is, due to their disagreement about the one from whom al-Qasim ibn al-Fadl narrates; and in either case he is unknown.

I say: Also, there is nothing in its chain indicating that Yusuf ibn Sa'd heard this from al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him. In the tafsir of al-Tabari, from 'Isa ibn Mazin, he said: "I said to al-Hasan: 'O blackener of the faces of the believers,'" up to the end of the hadith. And 'Isa ibn Mazin is not known at all. Even if we assume Yusuf ibn Sa'd is trustworthy, there is nothing in his narration requiring that he heard it; rather, it is possible that he intended to mention a story reported from al-Hasan.

The scholars of hadith have unanimously agreed that it is a munkar hadith; Ibn Kathir stated this and cited it from his teacher al-Mizzi. I say: its meaning is corrupt and the marks of fabrication are clear upon it, and it is from the fabrication of the sects that oppose the community (jama'ah). Therefore, relying on it is not fitting for such a thing to proceed from al-Hasan, given his great knowledge and acumen, and what connection is there between what they claim of the Messenger of Allah's ﷺ dream and al-Hasan's repelling of reproach from himself? There is no doubt that this report is a fabrication of the propagandists of the 'Abbasids, since it contradicts the facts: the period between al-Hasan's handing over the caliphate to Mu'awiyah and the pledge of allegiance to al-Saffah, the first of the 'Abbasid caliphs, is one thousand and ninety-two months or more by a month or two. So what is attributed to al-Qasim al-Huddani of his saying "we counted it and found it..." etc. is undoubtedly a lie.

Page 461
The conclusion is that this report which al-Tirmidhi related is munkar, as al-Mizzi said.

Ibn 'Arafa said: In His saying, ﴿The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months﴾, there is the embellishment called tashabuh al-atraf, which is the repetition of the rhyming word in the sentence that follows, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Like a niche within which is a lamp, the lamp within a glass, the glass as if it were a pearly star﴾ [al-Nur: 35]. End quote. He means by "rhyming word" what includes the qarinah in saj' and the fawasil in the verses. An example of it in poetry is the saying of Layla al-Akhyaliyyah:

"When al-Hajjaj descends upon a sick land, he tracks down its deepest disease and cures it.

He cures it of the incurable disease that afflicts it: a youth who, when he shakes the spear, gives it drink..."
Etc.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 97, verses 4–5 (part 1 of 2):

﴿The angels and the Spirit descend therein by permission of their Lord, with every decree.﴾ ﴿Peace it is until the emergence of dawn.﴾

When this second explanation is combined with the grandeur of ambiguity in His saying, ﴿And what can make you know what the Night of Decree is?﴾ [al-Qadr: 2], there results from it a clear indication that God has granted a similar excellence to every night of the years that falls on a night like this one, in the month in which the Qur'an was revealed, as an honour to the Qur'an, to the one upon whom it was sent down, to the religion in which it was sent down, and to the community that follows it. Do you not see that most of the surah is devoted to mentioning the virtues of the Night of Decree? It is only to encourage the seeking of righteous deeds during it. Its being better than a thousand months hints at this, and the sound reports clarify it. The use of the present tense in His saying, ﴿The angels descend﴾, indicates that this descent recurs in the future after the revelation of this surah.

Mentioning its end at the emergence of dawn has no bearing on explaining its excellence. It is therefore established that this is an insertion (idmaj) to define its limit, so that people will be eager to increase their deeds during it before it ends.

Indeed, the Night of Decree in which the revelation of the Qur'an began passed before anyone was aware of it except Muhammad (ﷺ), since he had been practising seclusion (tahannuth) during it, and the first of the Qur'an was revealed to him in its final part, and he returned to his family in its morning. Had it not been the intention to define the excellence of the nights that correspond to it in every year, it would have restricted itself to explaining the excellence of that first night. And since there was no need for the descent of the angels during it, nor for specifying its limit...

This is an instruction to the Muslims to venerate the days of their religious blessings and the days of God's favours upon them. It is similar to what God prescribed for Moses regarding the distinction of certain days of the years that correspond to days on which great favours of God were bestowed upon Moses. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And remind them of the days of God﴾ [Ibrahim: 5]. Accordingly, the Night of Decree should be counted as the festival of the revelation of the Qur'an.

The wisdom in concealing its precise identification is the intention that Muslims multiply their good deeds over many nights, seeking to coincide with the Night of Decree, just as the hour of answered supplication on Friday was concealed.

This is the essence of what the Qur'an has conveyed about the excellence of the Night of Decree every year, and it did not specify which night it is, nor from which month, although He, exalted is He, said: ﴿The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was sent down﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185]. Thus it becomes clear that the first Night of Decree is definitely one of the nights of the month of Ramadan. We may therefore seek to identify the first Night of Decree, in which the sending down of the Qur'an began, in order to seek out what corresponds to it among the nights of Ramadan in all years, and to determine the aspect of this correspondence. Correspondence occurs in various attributes, so it is not permissible that it correspond to it in the name of its day, such as Tuesday or Wednesday, nor in the season of winter or summer or the like, which are not among the circumstances considered in religion. Rather, we must seek an aspect of correspondence to it in the consideration of religion and in what pleases God. The determination of this correspondence has been greatly disputed, and the most sound position relied upon in this is that it is among the nights of the month of Ramadan in every year, and that it is among the odd nights, as indicated by the sound hadith: "Seek the Night of Decree among the odd nights of the last ten nights of Ramadan."

The odd (witr) is the most excellent of numbers in the sight of God, as indicated by the hadith: "God is odd and loves the odd." It is also not a fixed particular night recurring in every year; rather, it shifts from year to year, and it falls in Ramadan. This is the view of Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, and most scholars. Ibn Rashid said: "This is the soundest of the opinions and the most correct of them." On the basis that it shifts from year to year, most scholars hold that it does not leave the month of Ramadan. The majority hold that it does not leave the last ten nights of it, while a group said: it does not leave the middle ten nights or the last ten nights.

Those who narrated the reports specifying it interpreted them as meaning the usual case, or as referring to a particular year.

Nothing explicit concerning its identification has been transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ), because what has been reported on this subject from the reports is open to the interpretation that he meant its identification in the specific year about which he informed, and this is elaborated in the books of Sunnah, so we will not lengthen the discussion with it. Ibn Kathir has cited much of it.

It has been transmitted from Shaykh Muhyi al-Din ibn al-'Arabi that he specified its identification according to the variation of years in verses, mentioning in the final verse of them his saying:

"Its determining factor, by statement, is a Friday night that meets you after the midpoint, in an odd night."

We learned this from some of our teachers, and I have not found it. We tested the sign of the sunlight on its morning, and it did not fail.

The original form of tanazzalu is tatanazzalu, and one of the two tā' was elided for brevity. It is evident that the descent of the angels is to the earth.

The descent of the angels to the earth is for the sake of the blessings that surround them.

And al-Ruh (the Spirit) is Gabriel, meaning that Gabriel descends among the angels.

The meaning of "by permission of their Lord" is that this descent is an honour with which God has honoured the Muslims, in that He sent down to them on that night groups of His angels, and among them the most noble of them. Gabriel's descending on that night was so that the excellence which occurred on the first night, the night of his descent with revelation in the cave of Hira', would return to it in its correspondence.

In this is a basis for holding processions to commemorate the days of the glory and excellence of Islam, and that whoever has a role in the origin of that commemoration should not be absent from the procession of joy in recalling it.

His saying, "by permission of their Lord," is connected to "descend." It may be in the sense of causation, meaning: they descend because of the permission of their Lord granted to them to descend, so "permission" here is in the sense of the verbal noun (masdar). Or it may be in the sense of accompaniment, meaning: they are accompanied by what their Lord has permitted, so "permission" here is in the sense of "what is permitted," by the usage of the verbal noun for the object, as in this is the creation of God.

[Page 464]

The "min" in His saying ﴿with every decree﴾ may be explanatory (bayaniyyah), explaining the "permission" in "by permission of their Lord," meaning: by the permission of their Lord, which is in every matter.

It may also be in the sense of "bi" (with), meaning: they descend with every decree, like His saying: ﴿they guard him by the command of God﴾ [al-Ra'd: 11], meaning: by the command of God. This applies if the "bi" in "bi-idhni rabbihim" is causal. It may also be for causation (ta'lil), meaning: for the sake of every decree that God intended to execute through their subjugation.

The word "kull" (every) is used in the sense of multiplicity for the sake of importance, meaning: in many great matters, like His saying: ﴿And even if every sign came to them﴾ [Yunus: 97], and His saying: ﴿They will come to you on foot and on every lean camel﴾ [al-Hajj: 27], and His saying: ﴿And strike every fingertip of them﴾ [al-Anfal: 12], and the words of al-Nabighah:

"With them every ... and a doe grazing
toward every trembling one of the sand, solitary."

We have explained this at His saying: ﴿and on every lean camel﴾ [al-Hajj: 27] in the surah of al-Hajj.

The tanwin of "amr" (decree) is for magnification, meaning: with kinds of reward for deeds in that night. This decree is not the same as the decree in His saying: ﴿In it every wise matter is decreed﴾ [al-Dukhan: 4], although "a command from Us" in surah al-Dukhan is unified with a difference in its affairs, for it has many affairs.

It is possible that it is the decree mentioned here, so it is absolute here and restricted in the verse of al-Dukhan.

Know that the position of His saying, ﴿The angels and the Spirit descend therein﴾ up to His saying ﴿with every decree﴾, within the sentence ﴿The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months﴾ [al-Qadr: 3], is the position of the explanatory resumption (al-istinaf al-bayani), or the position of the substitute of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal). For the sake of observing this position, the sentence was separated from the one before it and not joined to it by a conjunction, although both of them share in the fact that each one conveys an explanation of the sentence ﴿And what can make you know what the Night of Decree is?﴾ [al-Qadr: 2]. The observance of its resumptive or substitutive position was preferred over observing their shared function as an explanation of ﴿And what can make you know what the Night of Decree is?﴾ [al-Qadr: 2], because this explanation is not lost on the hearer when it is presented in the form of explanation or substitution, unlike if it were conjoined to the preceding sentence by "wa" (and), since the indication would be lost that the descent of the angels therein is among the circumstances of its excellence.

The sentence ﴿Peace it is until the emergence of dawn﴾ is an explanation of the content of "with every decree," and it is in the manner of a precaution (ihtiras), because the descent of the angels occurs for good and may occur for evil, for the punishment of those who deny the messengers. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿We do not send down the angels except with truth, and then they would not be given respite﴾ [al-Hijr: 8]. And He said: ﴿On the day they see the angels, there will be no good news that day for the criminals﴾ [al-Furqan: 22]. He combined their descent for good and evil in His saying: ﴿When your Lord revealed to the angels, "I am with you, so strengthen those who have believed. I will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved, so strike above the necks"﴾ [al-Anfal: 12], and so on. Here He informed that the descent of the angels on the Night of Decree is to execute the command of good for the Muslims who fasted Ramadan and stood in prayer during the Night of Decree. This is therefore good tidings.

"Salam" (peace) is a verbal noun or a noun of the verbal noun, meaning safety, as He said: ﴿We said, "O fire, be coolness and safety upon Abraham"﴾ [al-Anbiya': 69]. "Salam" is also used for greeting and praise, and it has been interpreted as good. Both meanings are present in this verse. Safety encompasses every good, because good is safety from evil and harm, so "peace" includes forgiveness, abundant reward, and the answering of supplication for the good of this world and the Hereafter. "Salam" in the sense of greeting and good speech is intended to mean the praise of the angels upon the people of the Night of Decree, in accordance with their conduct with the people of Paradise, as reported in His saying: ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate, "Peace be upon you for what you patiently endured; how excellent is the final home"﴾ [al-Ra'd: 23–24].

The indefiniteness of "salam" (peace) is for magnification. He described the night as "peace" for emphasis, because it is a report using the verbal noun.

The fronting of the predicate, which is "salam," over the subject, which is the night, is for the purpose of exclusivity, meaning: it is nothing but peace. The restriction is claimed ( idda'i), because what happens therein to those who do not fast and stand in prayer is not counted. Then "salam hiya" may be intended merely as a report. It may also be intended as a command, with the estimated meaning: "Be at peace, a peace," so the verbal noun substitutes for the verb, and its being put in the nominative rather than the accusative is to convey stability, like His saying: ﴿They said, "Peace." He said, "Peace"﴾ [Hud: 69]. The meaning is: make it a peace among you, that is, no dispute and no quarrelling. This is indicated by what is in the sound hadith: "I came out to inform you of the Night of Decree, but two men quarrelled, so it was lifted. Perhaps it is better for you. So seek it on the ninth, the seventh, and the fifth."

And "until the emergence of dawn" is the limit of what precedes it, from His saying: ﴿The angels descend﴾ up to ﴿it is peace﴾.

The purpose of the limit is to convey that all the times of that night are filled with the descent of the angels and with peace. The limit here is therefore emphatic regarding the meaning of "night," because "night" may be applied to part of it, as in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever stands in prayer during the Night of Decree out of faith and seeking reward, his previous sins will be forgiven," meaning: whoever stands in prayer during part of it. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: "Whoever attends the 'isha' prayer on the night of Decree has taken his share of it." He means that he attended it in congregation, as the verb "attended" implies, for attending congregation is among the most excellent righteous deeds.

The particle "until" (hatta) is used to include the limit, to show that the Night of Decree extends beyond the emergence of dawn, such that the dawn prayer is considered to fall within that night, lest it be supposed that its end is like the end of the fast, at the last part of the night. This is an expansion from God in the extension of the night to what follows the emergence of dawn.

The benefit drawn from the purpose of the angels' descent in it is that this is the aim of the night, and the aim of the righteous deeds done in it that follow from its being better than a thousand months, and the aim of the peace that is in it.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read (مَطْلَعِ) with a fatha on the lam, as a mīmī (a verbal noun formed with an initial mīm), meaning the rising of the dawn, that is, its appearance. Al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with a kasra on the lam, meaning the time of the rising of the dawn.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

Surah al-Bayyinah

The name of this surah occurs in the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): (﴿Those who disbelieved would not...﴾ [Al-Bayyinah: 1]).

Al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated from Anas ibn Malik that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "Indeed Allah commanded me to recite to you (﴿Those who disbelieved would not...﴾ [Al-Bayyinah: 1])." He said: "And did He name me to you?" He said: "Yes." Then he wept.

His saying "to recite to you (﴿Those who disbelieved would not...﴾ [Al-Bayyinah: 1])" clearly means the whole surah, so he named it by its first sentence. In most books of tafsir (exegesis) and books of Sunnah, this surah is called Surat (Lam Yakun), by limiting the name to its first word. This name is the well-known one in Tunisia among the children of the katatib (Qur'anic schools).

In most copies of the Qur'an it is called Surat al-Qayyimah, and likewise in some tafsir works. In some copies of the Qur'an it is called Surat al-Bayyinah.

It is mentioned in al-Itqan that in the codex of Ubayy it was called Surat Ahl al-Kitab, that is, because of His saying: (﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book...﴾ [Al-Bayyinah: 1]). It was also called Surat al-Bariyyah and Surat al-Infikak. These are six names.

It has been disputed whether it is Meccan or Medinan. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The more well-known view is that it is Meccan, and this is the view of the majority of the commentators." From Ibn al-Zubayr and 'Ata' ibn Yasar it is reported that it is Medinan.

Al-Qurtubi reversed this, attributing the view that it is Medinan to the majority and to Ibn 'Abbas, and the view that it is Meccan to Yahya ibn Sallam. Ibn Kathir narrated from Ahmad ibn Hanbal, with his chain, to Abu Hibba al-Badri, who said: ("When the verse ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book...﴾ [Al-Bayyinah: 1] was revealed to its end, Jibril said: 'O Messenger of Allah, indeed Allah commands you to recite it to Ubayy'") — the hadith. That is, Ubayy was from the people of Medina. Al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir firmly held that it is Medinan, and this is the more apparent view because of the abundance in it of the rebuke of the People of the Book, and because of the hadith of Abu Hibba al-Badri. Jabir ibn Zayd also counted it among the Medinan surahs.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was only driven to contend with the People of the Book in Medina."

It is counted as the hundred and first in the order of revelation: it was revealed after Surat al-Talaq and before Surat al-Hashr. Therefore it was revealed before the expedition against the Banu al-Nadir, and the expedition against al-Nadir was in the fourth year (AH), in Rabi' al-Awwal. So the descent of this surah was at the end of the third year or the beginning of the fourth year.

Interwoven with all this is an exalting of the Qur'an and its excellence over other scriptures, through its including what is in the divine books that the Messenger (ﷺ) brought before it, together with what it contains of excellence and addition.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 97, verses 4–5 (part 1 of 2):

﴿The angels and the Spirit descend therein by permission of their Lord, with every decree.﴾ ﴿Peace it is until the emergence of dawn.﴾

When this second explanation is combined with the grandeur of ambiguity in His saying, ﴿And what can make you know what the Night of Decree is?﴾ [al-Qadr: 2], there results from it a clear indication that God has granted a similar excellence to every night of the years that falls on a night like this one, in the month in which the Qur'an was revealed, as an honour to the Qur'an, to the one upon whom it was sent down, to the religion in which it was sent down, and to the community that follows it. Do you not see that most of the surah is devoted to mentioning the virtues of the Night of Decree? It is only to encourage the seeking of righteous deeds during it. Its being better than a thousand months hints at this, and the sound reports clarify it. The use of the present tense in His saying, ﴿The angels descend﴾, indicates that this descent recurs in the future after the revelation of this surah.

Mentioning its end at the emergence of dawn has no bearing on explaining its excellence. It is therefore established that this is an insertion (idmaj) to define its limit, so that people will be eager to increase their deeds during it before it ends.

Indeed, the Night of Decree in which the revelation of the Qur'an began passed before anyone was aware of it except Muhammad (ﷺ), since he had been practising seclusion (tahannuth) during it, and the first of the Qur'an was revealed to him in its final part, and he returned to his family in its morning. Had it not been the intention to define the excellence of the nights that correspond to it in every year, it would have restricted itself to explaining the excellence of that first night. And since there was no need for the descent of the angels during it, nor for specifying its limit...

This is an instruction to the Muslims to venerate the days of their religious blessings and the days of God's favours upon them. It is similar to what God prescribed for Moses regarding the distinction of certain days of the years that correspond to days on which great favours of God were bestowed upon Moses. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And remind them of the days of God﴾ [Ibrahim: 5]. Accordingly, the Night of Decree should be counted as the festival of the revelation of the Qur'an.

The wisdom in concealing its precise identification is the intention that Muslims multiply their good deeds over many nights, seeking to coincide with the Night of Decree, just as the hour of answered supplication on Friday was concealed.

This is the essence of what the Qur'an has conveyed about the excellence of the Night of Decree every year, and it did not specify which night it is, nor from which month, although He, exalted is He, said: ﴿The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was sent down﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185]. Thus it becomes clear that the first Night of Decree is definitely one of the nights of the month of Ramadan. We may therefore seek to identify the first Night of Decree, in which the sending down of the Qur'an began, in order to seek out what corresponds to it among the nights of Ramadan in all years, and to determine the aspect of this correspondence. Correspondence occurs in various attributes, so it is not permissible that it correspond to it in the name of its day, such as Tuesday or Wednesday, nor in the season of winter or summer or the like, which are not among the circumstances considered in religion. Rather, we must seek an aspect of correspondence to it in the consideration of religion and in what pleases God. The determination of this correspondence has been greatly disputed, and the most sound position relied upon in this is that it is among the nights of the month of Ramadan in every year, and that it is among the odd nights, as indicated by the sound hadith: "Seek the Night of Decree among the odd nights of the last ten nights of Ramadan."

The odd (witr) is the most excellent of numbers in the sight of God, as indicated by the hadith: "God is odd and loves the odd." It is also not a fixed particular night recurring in every year; rather, it shifts from year to year, and it falls in Ramadan. This is the view of Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, and most scholars. Ibn Rashid said: "This is the soundest of the opinions and the most correct of them." On the basis that it shifts from year to year, most scholars hold that it does not leave the month of Ramadan. The majority hold that it does not leave the last ten nights of it, while a group said: it does not leave the middle ten nights or the last ten nights.

Those who narrated the reports specifying it interpreted them as meaning the usual case, or as referring to a particular year.

Nothing explicit concerning its identification has been transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ), because what has been reported on this subject from the reports is open to the interpretation that he meant its identification in the specific year about which he informed, and this is elaborated in the books of Sunnah, so we will not lengthen the discussion with it. Ibn Kathir has cited much of it.

It has been transmitted from Shaykh Muhyi al-Din ibn al-'Arabi that he specified its identification according to the variation of years in verses, mentioning in the final verse of them his saying:

"Its determining factor, by statement, is a Friday night that meets you after the midpoint, in an odd night."

We learned this from some of our teachers, and I have not found it. We tested the sign of the sunlight on its morning, and it did not fail.

The original form of tanazzalu is tatanazzalu, and one of the two tā' was elided for brevity. It is evident that the descent of the angels is to the earth.

The descent of the angels to the earth is for the sake of the blessings that surround them.

And al-Ruh (the Spirit) is Gabriel, meaning that Gabriel descends among the angels.

The meaning of "by permission of their Lord" is that this descent is an honour with which God has honoured the Muslims, in that He sent down to them on that night groups of His angels, and among them the most noble of them. Gabriel's descending on that night was so that the excellence which occurred on the first night, the night of his descent with revelation in the cave of Hira', would return to it in its correspondence.

In this is a basis for holding processions to commemorate the days of the glory and excellence of Islam, and that whoever has a role in the origin of that commemoration should not be absent from the procession of joy in recalling it.

His saying, "by permission of their Lord," is connected to "descend." It may be in the sense of causation, meaning: they descend because of the permission of their Lord granted to them to descend, so "permission" here is in the sense of the verbal noun (masdar). Or it may be in the sense of accompaniment, meaning: they are accompanied by what their Lord has permitted, so "permission" here is in the sense of "what is permitted," by the usage of the verbal noun for the object, as in this is the creation of God.

[Page 464]

The "min" in His saying ﴿with every decree﴾ may be explanatory (bayaniyyah), explaining the "permission" in "by permission of their Lord," meaning: by the permission of their Lord, which is in every matter.

It may also be in the sense of "bi" (with), meaning: they descend with every decree, like His saying: ﴿they guard him by the command of God﴾ [al-Ra'd: 11], meaning: by the command of God. This applies if the "bi" in "bi-idhni rabbihim" is causal. It may also be for causation (ta'lil), meaning: for the sake of every decree that God intended to execute through their subjugation.

The word "kull" (every) is used in the sense of multiplicity for the sake of importance, meaning: in many great matters, like His saying: ﴿And even if every sign came to them﴾ [Yunus: 97], and His saying: ﴿They will come to you on foot and on every lean camel﴾ [al-Hajj: 27], and His saying: ﴿And strike every fingertip of them﴾ [al-Anfal: 12], and the words of al-Nabighah:

"With them every ... and a doe grazing
toward every trembling one of the sand, solitary."

We have explained this at His saying: ﴿and on every lean camel﴾ [al-Hajj: 27] in the surah of al-Hajj.

The tanwin of "amr" (decree) is for magnification, meaning: with kinds of reward for deeds in that night. This decree is not the same as the decree in His saying: ﴿In it every wise matter is decreed﴾ [al-Dukhan: 4], although "a command from Us" in surah al-Dukhan is unified with a difference in its affairs, for it has many affairs.

It is possible that it is the decree mentioned here, so it is absolute here and restricted in the verse of al-Dukhan.

Know that the position of His saying, ﴿The angels and the Spirit descend therein﴾ up to His saying ﴿with every decree﴾, within the sentence ﴿The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months﴾ [al-Qadr: 3], is the position of the explanatory resumption (al-istinaf al-bayani), or the position of the substitute of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal). For the sake of observing this position, the sentence was separated from the one before it and not joined to it by a conjunction, although both of them share in the fact that each one conveys an explanation of the sentence ﴿And what can make you know what the Night of Decree is?﴾ [al-Qadr: 2]. The observance of its resumptive or substitutive position was preferred over observing their shared function as an explanation of ﴿And what can make you know what the Night of Decree is?﴾ [al-Qadr: 2], because this explanation is not lost on the hearer when it is presented in the form of explanation or substitution, unlike if it were conjoined to the preceding sentence by "wa" (and), since the indication would be lost that the descent of the angels therein is among the circumstances of its excellence.

The sentence ﴿Peace it is until the emergence of dawn﴾ is an explanation of the content of "with every decree," and it is in the manner of a precaution (ihtiras), because the descent of the angels occurs for good and may occur for evil, for the punishment of those who deny the messengers. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿We do not send down the angels except with truth, and then they would not be given respite﴾ [al-Hijr: 8]. And He said: ﴿On the day they see the angels, there will be no good news that day for the criminals﴾ [al-Furqan: 22]. He combined their descent for good and evil in His saying: ﴿When your Lord revealed to the angels, "I am with you, so strengthen those who have believed. I will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved, so strike above the necks"﴾ [al-Anfal: 12], and so on. Here He informed that the descent of the angels on the Night of Decree is to execute the command of good for the Muslims who fasted Ramadan and stood in prayer during the Night of Decree. This is therefore good tidings.

"Salam" (peace) is a verbal noun or a noun of the verbal noun, meaning safety, as He said: ﴿We said, "O fire, be coolness and safety upon Abraham"﴾ [al-Anbiya': 69]. "Salam" is also used for greeting and praise, and it has been interpreted as good. Both meanings are present in this verse. Safety encompasses every good, because good is safety from evil and harm, so "peace" includes forgiveness, abundant reward, and the answering of supplication for the good of this world and the Hereafter. "Salam" in the sense of greeting and good speech is intended to mean the praise of the angels upon the people of the Night of Decree, in accordance with their conduct with the people of Paradise, as reported in His saying: ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate, "Peace be upon you for what you patiently endured; how excellent is the final home"﴾ [al-Ra'd: 23–24].

The indefiniteness of "salam" (peace) is for magnification. He described the night as "peace" for emphasis, because it is a report using the verbal noun.

The fronting of the predicate, which is "salam," over the subject, which is the night, is for the purpose of exclusivity, meaning: it is nothing but peace. The restriction is claimed ( idda'i), because what happens therein to those who do not fast and stand in prayer is not counted. Then "salam hiya" may be intended merely as a report. It may also be intended as a command, with the estimated meaning: "Be at peace, a peace," so the verbal noun substitutes for the verb, and its being put in the nominative rather than the accusative is to convey stability, like His saying: ﴿They said, "Peace." He said, "Peace"﴾ [Hud: 69]. The meaning is: make it a peace among you, that is, no dispute and no quarrelling. This is indicated by what is in the sound hadith: "I came out to inform you of the Night of Decree, but two men quarrelled, so it was lifted. Perhaps it is better for you. So seek it on the ninth, the seventh, and the fifth."

And "until the emergence of dawn" is the limit of what precedes it, from His saying: ﴿The angels descend﴾ up to ﴿it is peace﴾.

The purpose of the limit is to convey that all the times of that night are filled with the descent of the angels and with peace. The limit here is therefore emphatic regarding the meaning of "night," because "night" may be applied to part of it, as in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever stands in prayer during the Night of Decree out of faith and seeking reward, his previous sins will be forgiven," meaning: whoever stands in prayer during part of it. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: "Whoever attends the 'isha' prayer on the night of Decree has taken his share of it." He means that he attended it in congregation, as the verb "attended" implies, for attending congregation is among the most excellent righteous deeds.

The particle "until" (hatta) is used to include the limit, to show that the Night of Decree extends beyond the emergence of dawn, such that the dawn prayer is considered to fall within that night, lest it be supposed that its end is like the end of the fast, at the last part of the night. This is an expansion from God in the extension of the night to what follows the emergence of dawn.

The benefit drawn from the purpose of the angels' descent in it is that this is the aim of the night, and the aim of the righteous deeds done in it that follow from its being better than a thousand months, and the aim of the peace that is in it.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read (مَطْلَعِ) with a fatha on the lam, as a mīmī (a verbal noun formed with an initial mīm), meaning the rising of the dawn, that is, its appearance. Al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with a kasra on the lam, meaning the time of the rising of the dawn.
